title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 27–28
description: Advanced tourist-destination promotion, natural scenery and travel experiences; climate, ecosystems, farming, industry and population descriptions with precise collocations and lexical contrasts.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Vocabulary and topics were checked against the teaching pages, exercises and answer key; Portuguese translations, usage notes and sample sentences were independently written. Original exercise text, textbook paragraphs and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Both Advanced Third Edition teaching pages and facing exercises for Units 27–28, destination advertisements, annotated glossary, region descriptions, exercises 27.1–27.4 and 28.1–28.5, and relevant answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is selectively provided for short targets where confident; multiword and otherwise unverified entries have empty IPA. Regional accents and connected speech are not fully represented.
audit.languagePolicy: English-only learner-facing prose, examples and metadata; Brazilian Portuguese appears only in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the PDF study pages, illustrations and exercises with the relevant answer key. Independently authored examples and notes and checked lexical distinctions, translations, item provenance, unique IDs, schema parity and TTS target readability. No live VocabLab import, browser TTS or speech-recognition testing was performed.
audit.limitations: No recorded audio is bundled (audio fields are empty). Browser import, synthesized word/sentence audio and speech-recognition behaviour require testing in VocabLab. Tourism adjectives may be promotional rather than objective; descriptions of national development and populations are context-sensitive.

units.title: Unit 27 — Attracting tourists
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 27. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Travel and tourism · destinations, travel advertising and natural attractions
learningObjectives: Describe less-visited destinations using idiomatic expressions about crowds, wilderness and unusual experiences.
Interpret promotional language, including formal travel-industry vocabulary and strong evaluative adjectives.
Distinguish ramble, hike and trek, and describe tourism that protects the natural environment.
Use authentic collocations such as boast attractions, a wealth of wildlife and large tracts of rainforest.

sectionsChecked: All teaching-page text, explanatory notes and travel advertisements or country descriptions
Facing exercises and corresponding answer-key entries
Register, nuanced collocations, word formation and meaning contrasts

items.pt: fugir das multidões; escapar de lugares cheios
items.example: We chose a quiet island to escape the crowds during the holiday season.
items.note: Suggests seeking a less busy destination, often in promotional travel writing.

items.pt: sair dos roteiros turísticos tradicionais; explorar lugares pouco visitados
items.example: Travellers can get off the beaten track by exploring the inland villages.
items.note: Idiomatic expression for visiting places that are not popular tourist routes.

items.pt: voltar a ter contato com a natureza
items.example: After months in the city, they wanted to get back to nature.
items.note: Means spending time in natural surroundings and away from urban routines.

items.example: Investment in the tourist sector has created jobs in rural districts.
items.note: Formal economic term for businesses and services related to tourism.

items.example: The boutique lodge appeals to the discerning traveller who values privacy.
items.note: Discerning implies well-developed judgement about quality or style, not simply wealthy.

items.pt: ter como atrativo; ostentar; orgulhar-se de oferecer
items.example: The region boasts an impressive network of walking trails.
items.note: In destination descriptions, boast introduces appealing features of a place; often promotional or formal.

items.example: Hordes of visitors arrive at the small harbour every summer.
items.note: Hordes of people has a negative connotation of unwelcome numbers.

items.pt: grande riqueza de vida selvagem; abundância de fauna
items.example: The wetlands support a wealth of wildlife throughout the year.
items.note: A wealth of means a large amount of something valuable, not necessarily money.

items.example: The reserve protects the region’s distinctive flora and fauna.
items.note: Fixed paired expression for the plants and animals of an area.

items.example: The national park limits vehicle access to protect fragile habitats.
items.note: A legally protected area valued for scenery, nature or heritage; rules differ by country.

items.example: The coastal nature reserve provides a breeding ground for rare birds.
items.note: A protected area especially associated with conserving species and habitats.

items.pt: extensão de terra; vasta área de terreno
items.example: A vast tract of land remains inaccessible by road.
items.note: Often large or vast tracts of land; a formal way to describe an extensive area.

items.pt: floresta tropical intocada; floresta úmida primária
items.example: Researchers surveyed a stretch of virgin rainforest that had never been logged.
items.note: Virgin here means previously untouched or undisturbed, not newly planted.

items.word: seek something out of the ordinary
items.example: Adventurous guests seek something out of the ordinary when choosing a destination.
items.note: Seek is relatively formal; out of the ordinary describes something unusual.

items.pt: algo fora do comum; algo incomum
items.example: The guided night walk offered something out of the ordinary.
items.note: A fixed evaluative phrase; it can be positive or simply describe an unusual experience.

items.example: Quiet observation is the best way to see the island’s wildlife.
items.note: A collective uncountable noun for wild animals living in a place.

items.example: The tourism industry supports many local guides and small businesses.
items.note: A common alternative to the more formal tourist sector; not the same as a single tour company.

items.example: She went hiking at the coast to unwind after a demanding project.
items.note: Informal-to-neutral verb for relaxing and reducing tension.

items.pt: recarregar as energias; recuperar a disposição
items.example: A long weekend in the countryside helped him recharge his batteries.
items.note: Metaphor meaning regain physical or mental energy, not literally charge a device.

items.pt: área selvagem coberta por vegetação; mato
items.example: The lodge organises guided walks through the bush.
items.note: Especially used in African and Australian settings for wild, vegetated country away from cities.

items.pt: veículo com tração nas quatro rodas; veículo 4x4
items.example: The guide recommended a four-by-four for the final stretch of the journey.
items.note: Written as 4x4 and pronounced four by four; a vehicle with driving power on all four wheels.

items.pt: à beira-mar; à margem de um rio ou lago
items.example: They booked a waterfront apartment overlooking the harbour.
items.note: As a modifier, waterfront refers to property at the edge of a body of water.

items.example: The viewpoint offers stunning panoramas of the valley.
items.note: Strongly positive, frequently used in tourism and promotional writing.

items.example: The travel agency advertised unbeatable prices for winter breaks.
items.note: Promotional claim that competitors cannot offer better prices for comparable services.

items.example: The sheer scale of the canyon was awe-inspiring.
items.note: Suggests a powerful feeling of wonder at grandeur, power or beauty.

items.pt: caminhada tranquila e longa, geralmente no campo
items.example: We went for a gentle ramble across the fields after lunch.
items.note: Typically a pleasant, unhurried country walk; less physically demanding than a hike or trek.

items.example: The six-hour hike took us over rocky terrain.
items.note: Usually more physically demanding than a ramble; may involve hills or rough ground.

items.pt: travessia longa a pé; caminhada de vários dias
items.example: They planned a week-long trek through a remote mountain range.
items.note: Often a lengthy and demanding journey on foot, over wild country.

items.example: The region offers unrivalled opportunities for birdwatching.
items.note: Promotional, strong positive adjective meaning no other option matches it; British spelling.

items.example: We took the scenic route along the coast rather than the motorway.
items.note: Used for routes and views with attractive natural scenery.

items.example: The brochure described the secluded bay as a tropical paradise.
items.note: Typical idealising phrase in travel advertising; paradise is figurative.

items.example: Local guides hope ecotourism will finance forest conservation.
items.note: Tourism intended to benefit communities and limit environmental harm; promotional claims deserve scrutiny.

items.example: Take a moment to savour the view before continuing the climb.
items.note: More evocative or formal than enjoy; also used for tastes and experiences.

items.pt: região central; interior considerado o núcleo de um país
items.example: The tour explores the agricultural heartland of the country.
items.note: The central or defining inland region; can be geographic or figurative.

items.example: Visitors travel from abroad to admire the area’s renowned landscapes.
items.note: Renowned is a formal positive word meaning widely known and admired.

units.title: Unit 28 — Describing the world
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 28. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: World and environment · climate, vegetation, agriculture, industry and population
learningObjectives: Describe regions accurately using climate, rainfall, drought and landscape vocabulary.
Contrast vegetation zones and types of forests, and use precise agricultural collocations.
Discuss manufacturing and development with appropriate economic terminology and register.
Distinguish ancestors, descendants, migrants, emigrants and immigrants in population descriptions.

sectionsChecked: All teaching-page text, explanatory notes and travel advertisements or country descriptions
Facing exercises and corresponding answer-key entries
Register, nuanced collocations, word formation and meaning contrasts

items.pt: precipitação de chuva; volume de chuva
items.example: Annual rainfall varies significantly between the coast and the interior.
items.note: Measured amount of rain over a period; can be high or low.

items.example: Rivers rise rapidly during the wet season.
items.note: Period of the year with heavier rainfall; contrasts with dry season.

items.example: The plateau is too arid to support intensive farming without irrigation.
items.note: Formal adjective for very dry land or climate.

items.pt: ser propenso a; estar sujeito a
items.example: Low-lying districts are prone to flooding after heavy rain.
items.note: Typically followed by a negative event or condition, such as drought or flooding.

items.example: A prolonged drought caused severe water shortages in the region.
items.note: Long period with little or no rainfall; compare a brief dry spell.

items.example: The reserve restricts open fires during the dry season.
items.note: Part of the year with less rainfall; the opposite of wet season in this context.

items.example: Parts of northern Scandinavia lie within the Arctic Circle.
items.note: Geographic circle in the far northern hemisphere, not a type of ecosystem.

items.pt: tundra; região fria com pouca ou nenhuma árvore
items.example: Low-growing plants survive during the short summer on the tundra.
items.note: Cold treeless biome, often with frozen ground.

items.example: Dense vegetation concealed the entrance to the old footpath.
items.note: Collective term for the plant life of an area; generally uncountable.

items.example: A dense forest covers much of the mountain’s lower slopes.
items.note: Dense describes thickly packed plants or trees.

items.example: A coniferous forest surrounds the mountain research station.
items.note: Conifers usually have cones and needle-like foliage; many are evergreen.

items.pt: perene; que mantém folhas durante todo o ano
items.example: The evergreen trees retain their leaves through winter.
items.note: Contrasts with deciduous, although not all evergreens are conifers.

items.pt: caducifólio; que perde as folhas em determinada estação
items.example: Deciduous trees shed their leaves before the coldest months.
items.note: Opposite of evergreen in this context; emphasis is seasonal leaf loss.

items.example: Much of northern Canada is covered by taiga.
items.note: Broad subarctic forest zone, often dominated by conifers.

items.pt: campos; pradarias; extensões dominadas por gramíneas
items.example: Grazing animals move across the grasslands as the seasons change.
items.note: Plural landscape term for regions dominated by grasses.

items.pt: pradaria; campo plano da América do Norte
items.example: Wild grasses cover much of the prairie in early summer.
items.note: North American term; compare steppe and pampas in other regions.

items.pt: estepe; campo seco de clima continental
items.example: Nomadic herders traditionally travelled across the Eurasian steppe.
items.note: Wide open grassland, often in drier continental climates.

items.example: Cattle farming is prominent on the Argentine pampas.
items.note: South American grasslands; commonly used with the definite article.

items.example: The temperate forest supports both broadleaf and conifer species.
items.note: Located in regions with relatively moderate seasonal climates.

items.example: The farmers grow a second crop after the main harvest.
items.note: Can mean a cultivated plant or the resulting harvest; context determines the sense.

items.example: The village is surrounded by paddy fields fed by irrigation canals.
items.note: Flooded field used for growing rice; paddy and paddy field are not the same as any field.

items.example: Workers harvest the rice once the grains have matured.
items.note: Both noun and verb, referring to collecting a cultivated crop.

items.example: Wheat and barley are cereals grown in cooler climates.
items.note: Grain-producing grasses such as wheat, maize and rice; plural is common for the category.

items.pt: cuidar do rebanho; tratar de animais de criação
items.example: Several families still tend livestock on the hillsides.
items.note: Tend is relatively literary or formal for look after; usually tend sheep or cattle in the unit.

items.example: The farmer moved the cattle to higher ground before the flood.
items.note: Plural collective noun; one cow or one head of cattle, not a cattle.

items.pt: pastor de ovelhas; pessoa que cuida de um rebanho ovino
items.example: A shepherd led the flock down from the mountains.
items.note: Someone whose job is to look after sheep.

items.pt: plantação de grande escala; propriedade agrícola de cultivo comercial
items.example: The old tea plantation now also welcomes visitors.
items.note: Large estate devoted to a cash crop; e.g. tea, coffee, sugar or rubber.

items.example: A developed nation may still have significant regional inequality.
items.note: Source terminology for a country with a modern industrial economy; economic classifications vary.

items.example: The programme supports engineering training in developing countries.
items.note: Broad economic category used in the source; context-sensitive and not a universal fixed classification.

items.example: Manufacturing industry remains important in the region’s economy.
items.note: Production of goods on an industrial scale; distinguish from services or extraction.

items.example: The chemical industry supplies materials for many other sectors.
items.note: Industrial sector producing chemicals and chemical products.

items.pt: indústria siderúrgica; setor de produção de aço
items.example: Employment in the steel industry fell after several plants closed.
items.note: The industrial sector producing steel.

items.pt: estar na vanguarda de; ocupar posição de destaque
items.example: The institute is at the forefront of renewable-energy research.
items.note: At the forefront of means holding a leading position in an area.

items.example: The new port required a sizeable public investment.
items.note: British spelling; American sizeable or sizable; means fairly large.

items.example: The nuclear industry requires specialised safety systems.
items.note: Industrial activities associated with nuclear technology and power generation.

items.example: The turbines generate electricity for nearby communities.
items.note: Technical collocation; generate can also be used for income and interest.

items.pt: uma parcela significativa; uma proporção expressiva
items.example: Renewables provide a significant proportion of the area’s power.
items.note: Formal quantitative collocation, especially in statistics or reports.

items.pt: prestar auxílio; fornecer ajuda ou assistência
items.example: Several agencies provide aid after major natural disasters.
items.note: Aid may include money, supplies or practical assistance, not only development loans.

items.pt: mistura vibrante; combinação dinâmica e diversa
items.example: The city is a vibrant mixture of languages and traditions.
items.note: Positive evaluative collocation for a lively blend of different elements.

items.example: Her family is descended from migrants who arrived a century ago.
items.note: Genealogical expression followed by a person or group from the past.

items.example: The exhibition highlights the knowledge of indigenous communities.
items.note: Of peoples or organisms originating in a particular place; use respectful context-specific terms.

items.example: The former colonial power controlled the island’s ports for decades.
items.note: A state exercising political authority over a colonised territory.

items.example: One of her ancestors migrated to the country in the nineteenth century.
items.note: Relative from an earlier generation, not a person descended from you.

items.example: Many descendants of the original settlers still live in the valley.
items.note: Person descended from a predecessor or ancestor; opposite genealogical direction to ancestor.

items.pt: migrante; pessoa que se desloca para morar em outro lugar
items.example: Seasonal migrants often travel long distances to find work.
items.note: General term for someone moving within or between countries; direction is not inherent.

items.pt: emigrante; pessoa que sai do próprio país para morar fora
items.example: The emigrant left Portugal to start a new life in Brazil.
items.note: Emigrant is viewed from the country being left.

items.pt: imigrante; pessoa que chega a outro país para morar nele
items.example: The immigrant settled in the city after finding employment.
items.note: Immigrant is viewed from the country entered.

items.example: Many families settled in the region after the new railway opened.
items.note: Settle in a place means establish a home there, not merely visit.

items.pt: plantação de café; fazenda cafeeira de grande escala
items.example: The coffee plantation sells part of its harvest to local roasters.
items.note: Exercise-supported alternative to tea, sugar and rubber plantation.

items.example: The pharmaceutical industry invests heavily in clinical research.
items.note: Industrial sector developing and manufacturing medicines.

items.pt: campo petrolífero; jazida de petróleo explorada
items.example: Engineers developed an offshore oil field near the coast.
items.note: A geographic area containing exploitable oil deposits; unlike paddy field.

items.example: A sovereign nation is able to make its own laws and foreign-policy decisions.
items.note: Sovereign stresses political independence; distinct from simply developed.

items.example: The instrument measures changes in the local magnetic field.
items.note: Field here refers to a physical influence, not agricultural land.
